why: The on-screen caption admits it: "A fictional satirical promotion."
It carries Content Credentials from OpenAI. Run it through Check an image and you'll see the AI label.
The logos, station branding, and on-screen text all look right. Today's tools render text well, so the clue is the story itself: a bank CEO announcing free cookies on live TV.
ai.context: Fake news broadcasts featuring real executives are used to promote scams and fake giveaways.

There are no obvious giveaways here. The skin, hair, and background all hold up to close inspection. That's why visual checks alone aren't enough: a reverse image search and a watermark check are more reliable.

why: Everything feels staged, like a catalogue shoot: every person is posed perfectly with a camera-ready smile, the lighting is flawless, and the room looks like a furniture showroom rather than a lived-in home.
The portraits on the walls are generic "old master" paintings of the kind AI tools use to signal a wealthy setting.
The text on the book cover on the coffee table is unreadable.
Its metadata labels it as made with a Google AI tool. Check an image will show this label.
ai.context: Who is in a photo is never a good clue on its own. Real families come in every combination. Look instead for things that are too perfect or that don't hold together.

why: It carries Content Credentials from OpenAI. Run it through Check an image and you'll see the AI label.
The story itself is the biggest clue: a bank CEO announcing free cookies as breaking news.
ai.context: Fake news broadcasts featuring real executives are used to promote scams and fake giveaways.

why: Look closely at the logo patch on the hat: the lettering is slightly off.
Its metadata labels it as made with a Google AI tool. Check an image will show this label.
The film-style date stamp and grain make it feel like a casual, authentic snapshot. Effects like these are easy to add, so don't treat them as evidence.
The ticker at the bottom falls apart into gibberish: "No injuries have bed hıaen teported."
It carries Content Credentials from OpenAI. Run it through Check an image and you'll see the AI label.
The small handwritten signs look almost readable, but the words are garbled. AI tools handle large text, like the banner, much better than small text.
It carries Content Credentials marking it as AI-generated. Check an image will show the label.

ai.context: There are no obvious giveaways here. Even the outfitter's logo on the raft is clean and plausible, because current tools render text and logos well.

why: The text on the ID is mostly gibberish, and the name and address are unreadable.
Both dates on the card are from 2013, which doesn't fit the adult holding it.
The signature is an illegible scribble.
ai.context: "Selfie holding an ID" images like this are what attackers use to get past online identity checks when opening accounts. See How attackers use AI.

why: The wrinkles on the fingers don't follow the joints the way real skin creases do.
The thumbnail has an unnatural break running across it.
ai.context: "Impossibly cute" animal photos like this are a common way for accounts to build a following quickly, which can later be sold or used for scams.

why: Count the fingers on the hand on the right side of the picture: there are six.
The fingers blend into the dough where they press into it.
The woman on the right has an impossibly long neck.
The interlocked fingers don't add up. Count them and you'll find more than two hands should have, bent in ways real joints can't.
The row of colored squares in the bottom-right corner is the watermark OpenAI's DALL·E 2 added to its images.
The clasped hands show three thumbs and an impossible arrangement of fingers.
Elon Musk's facial features are slightly off compared with real photos of him.
ai.context: Realistic images of public figures in situations that never happened can damage reputations, move markets, and spread disinformation.

why: The road signs are garbled and don't match real French traffic signs.
Several people's shadows don't line up with the direction of the sunlight.
ai.context: Images like this circulated online as supposed photos of Paris during the 2023 sanitation workers' strike.

why: The fence and the building blend into each other, fading in and out along their length.
The lamp post has a faint ghost image that can't be explained by the lighting or the camera.
ai.context: In May 2023, this image spread on social media as a supposed explosion near the Pentagon. It was shared by verified accounts and briefly moved the US stock market before officials confirmed nothing had happened.

why: The two receipts were supposedly printed 24 years apart, yet they share the same store, address, and store number, and have the same pattern of creases.
The address doesn't exist: there is no Palm Grove Road store in "Sunset Bay, FL."
The items are generic ("CHKN BREAST," "COFFEE") rather than the specific brands and sizes a real receipt lists, and the bananas weigh exactly 3 pounds.
A watermark check identifies it as made with OpenAI's tools.
ai.context: Viral "then and now" comparisons like this are designed to provoke a reaction and get shared. Check before you share.

why: Look closely at her hands around the puppy: the fingers are malformed and hard to count.
ai.context: This image spread widely on social media after Hurricane Helene in 2024 as a supposed photo of the disaster.

why: A reverse image search (TinEye) finds the same man in the same shirt in other photos, a hallmark of romance scam profiles.
The laptop keyboard has too many keys in each row, and the space bar is split into several keys.
The cables don't make sense: the laptop's cable splits in two, one wire ends in mid-air, and another seems to pass through a notepad.
The hard hat hangs on a hook on what would be the outside of the door.
The oil platforms outside are implausibly close together, and the porthole is larger than a ship's porthole would be, with no visible seal against water.
There's a halo of pixelation around the man, the laptop, and the bed frame, a sign that he was pasted onto a different background.
A SynthID check finds Google's AI watermark.
ai.context: "Working on an oil rig" is a classic romance scam story. It explains why the person can't meet in person and sets up later requests for money.

why: The small text on the bags is gibberish. Look at the Morrisons bag on top of the pile.
The signs inside the store and on the wall above the trolleys are unreadable.
The trolley at the far right end of the row is facing backwards and merges into the others.
The legs of her folding chair don't connect in a way that makes sense.
The brick corner behind the trolleys gradually disappears as it goes down the wall.
The "handwritten" sign is unusually neat.
A faint watermark in the top-right corner comes from a humor site, a sign the image may be a joke passed off as real.
A SynthID check finds Google's AI watermark.
Count the legs: he has an extra one.
Look at her hands: they're feet. She's holding the tray with toes instead of fingers.
ai.context: The red circles are a misdirection. They point at harmless details in the background and pull your eye away from the real giveaway in plain sight. Don't let someone else's annotations decide where you look.

why: The chair in front of the cat has two backs, and the back of the cat's chair doesn't line up with its seat.
The layout doesn't work: a table sits between the bride and the officiant, and the groom is standing behind it instead of beside the bride.
The floorboard lines disappear in the middle of the aisle.
The seated guest's leg is misshapen, and the foot melts into the chair.
The bottom half of the window is out of proportion.
A watermark check identifies it as made with OpenAI's tools.
ai.context: Heartwarming stories like this are a common kind of engagement bait: images built to be liked and shared.

why: The playground equipment doesn't hold together: poles and platforms don't connect the way a real structure would.
ai.context: "John" doesn't exist. Ars Technica created him and, using just seven photos, trained an AI model to produce realistic fake images of him in compromising situations, like this shirtless selfie at a children's playground. A handful of public photos is enough to do the same to a real person.

source.title: Ars Technica, "AI image generation tech can now create life-wrecking deepfakes with ease" (December 2022)
